name: Microsoft Corporation
subcategory: software / cloud (Azure, Microsoft 365); developer platforms (.NET, VS Code, TypeScript, GitHub); AI (OpenAI partnership, Phi open models)
origin_detail: Founded in 1975 by Bill Gates and Paul Allen. Built on proprietary licensing (MS-DOS, Windows, Office); under Steve Ballmer it treated Linux and the GPL as a threat, then from 2014 under Satya Nadella re-oriented around Azure and open-source developer tools.
openness_notes: Scored on the AI and developer-platform strategy. Initial 0: proprietary platforms; in 2001 Ballmer called Linux 'a cancer that attaches itself in an intellectual property sense to everything it touches'. Current 2 (open core): the developer layer is largely OSI-licensed (.NET Core MIT with a patent promise from 2014-11-12, under the .NET Foundation formed at Build 2014; VS Code source MIT since Nov 2015; Copilot Chat extension MIT since 2025-06-30; Phi-4 weights MIT since 2025-01-08), but revenue comes from proprietary cloud and productivity services, the Copilot inline-completion extension and backend models stay closed, and its frontier AI comes from the closed OpenAI partnership. TypeScript is a flagship open project, but its licence history was not verified here because the search budget ran out.

license_history.note: Ballmer's 'Linux is a cancer' remark (aimed at the GPL's reach); in 2016 he said the Linux threat was 'in the rearview mirror' and praised SQL Server on Linux.
Announced 2014-11-12: runtime and framework libraries open source and cross-platform, contributed to the .NET Foundation (announced at Build 2014).
Open-sourced at Connect(); 2015 in November 2015 (date from a single aggregator report).

license_history.note: Phi-4 first offered in December 2024 on Azure AI Foundry under a research licence agreement.
Phi-4 weights on Hugging Face 2025-01-08 under MIT; Phi-4-reasoning (report 2025-04-30) also MIT.

license_history.note: Announced at Build 2025 (2025-05-19), code public 2025-06-30 at microsoft/vscode-copilot-chat; inline-completion extension and backend models remain closed.

relicensing_events.to: MIT-licensed, cross-platform .NET Core under the .NET Foundation
relicensing_events.outcome_note: The emblematic step of the Nadella-era turn toward open source and Linux, aligned with Azure's need to host Linux workloads.

relicensing_events.from: Phi-4 under a research licence on Azure only
relicensing_events.to: Phi-4 weights under MIT on Hugging Face
relicensing_events.outcome_note: Small-model line released under an OSI licence; Microsoft's frontier AI remains closed (OpenAI models).

relicensing_events.to: MIT-licensed Copilot Chat extension, being folded into VS Code core
relicensing_events.outcome_note: Presented as making VS Code an 'open source AI editor'; partial, since completions and models stay proprietary.

risk_events: 2001: Ballmer's 'Linux is a cancer' remark crystallised developer distrust that the later open-source turn had to overcome

2018-10-25: acquired GitHub in a $7.5B stock transaction (including $1.3B cash for vested GitHub equity awards and an indemnity escrow), putting the main hub of open-source development under one vendor; new CEO Nat Friedman pledged GitHub would operate independently in response to developer concerns
AI dependence on a closed partner: FY2026 net income included $4.963B of net gains from its OpenAI investment
FY2026: total headcount fell ~5,000 to ~223,000, the first annual decline in a decade (R&D down ~4,000 from the 2024 peak)
robustness: Highly diversified and profitable (FY2026 revenue $331.8B, net income $133.7B; Azure passed $100B). .NET sits in a foundation and VS Code, TypeScript and Phi are under permissive licences, so they can be forked, but Microsoft controls their roadmaps; the official VS Code builds and Copilot services are proprietary. Owning GitHub gives Microsoft a central position in the open-source supply chain.
physical_science_relevance: GitHub hosts most open research software; VS Code and Python tooling are standard in scientific computing; Phi models are small enough to run locally for lab use.
openness_effect_assessment: Microsoft's move from hostility (2001) to open-sourcing .NET (2014), VS Code (2015) and buying GitHub (2018) coincided with its pivot to the Azure cloud, where hosting open-source and Linux workloads was the business. Opening the developer layer won developer mindshare without giving up the proprietary cloud and productivity services that earn the money; by FY2026 Azure alone passed $100B. In AI it pairs a closed frontier partner (OpenAI) with MIT-licensed small models and tooling.
key_takeaway: Microsoft is the canonical convert: once its revenue moved from selling Windows licences to renting cloud capacity, open source changed from threat to on-ramp, and it open-sourced its developer stack and bought the platform where open source lives. Its openness is real at the tool and small-model layer and absent at the money-making core, an open-core strategy run at the scale of a $3.6T company. For the study it shows that a firm's stance on openness tracks where its profits come from, not ideology.
